Question six. Why do float thirty-two versus float sixty-four matter for ML data? Float thirty-two halves memory and bandwidth, and it's what GPUs run on. Ten million embeddings of a hundred and twenty-eight numbers take about five gigabytes in float thirty-two, and ten in float sixty-four. The price is precision: about seven significant digits. Add point one to a float thirty-two running total ten million times, and it ends at one million eighty-eight thousand, nine percent high. Near a million, each point one is rounded to an eighth. NumPy's own sum adds in pairs, and misses by only an eighth. So store big arrays in float thirty-two, and keep long running totals in float sixty-four.

Question seven. Why subtract the max before exponentiating in softmax? Float sixty-four tops out near e to the seven hundred and nine. Scores of a thousand, a thousand and one, and a thousand and two overflow to infinity, and infinity over infinity is not a number, three times. Softmax doesn't change when every score shifts by the same amount. Subtract the largest, and the biggest exponent is zero: nine, twenty-four and sixty-seven percent. One step further: the loss takes a log. Give the right class a score of a hundred against a thousand, and its probability underflows to zero, whose log is minus infinity. Log-softmax computes minus nine hundred directly, so a loss should take the raw scores.
